531.quote_or_event: “Though one believe in the Law, he will rarely practise it; for people are engrossed by pleasures; Gautama, &c.”
531.explanation: Mahavira warns Gautama that even those who hold the true teaching fail to act on it because pleasure absorbs them, and the refrain he repeats is 'be careful all the while'.
531.tie_back: The Kural says carelessness born of great joy does more harm than anger; Mahavira likewise names absorption in pleasure as what makes people neglect what they know.
531.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
531._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com ('&c.' abbreviates the refrain in the original). The comparison with anger is absent.

532.quote_or_event: “There are five causes which render wholesome discipline impossible: egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness”
532.explanation: Carelessness (pramada) is named among the forces that destroy a monk's discipline.
532.tie_back: Valluvar says forgetfulness kills a man's fame as poverty kills his intellect; the Jain text says carelessness kills the discipline on which a monk's worth rests.
532.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
532._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse is about discipline, not fame, and has no comparison with poverty.

533.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
533.explanation: This lecture repeats the single command 'be careful all the while' (do not be heedless, pamaya) at the end of nearly every verse, which makes heedfulness the constant burden of Mahavira's teaching.
533.tie_back: The Kural says every school of thought agrees that the heedless win no lasting glory; in the Jain canon heedfulness is likewise the teaching the master repeats without exception.
533.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
533._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse stresses heedfulness because life is fleeting, not because of fame or the agreement of all treatises.

534.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
534.explanation: Mahavira teaches that outward advantages are useless to the careless, who lose even the insight they once had.
534.tie_back: Valluvar says no advantage helps the heedless, just as no fortress helps the fearful; the Jain verse likewise says wealth cannot protect the careless.
534.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
534._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on outward goods being useless to the careless; the fortress simile is replaced by the image of a lamp going out.

535.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
535.explanation: The monk who puts off the work of self-mastery, assuming there is time, ends in despair when the end arrives.
535.tie_back: The Kural says the man who fails to guard against trouble in advance grieves over his mistake when it strikes; Mahavira describes the same belated despair of the procrastinator.
535.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
535._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (the bracketed phrase is Jacobi's). Strong fit on regret for neglect, though the trouble in question is death, not an enemy.

536.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhârunda bird!”
536.explanation: Mahavira asks for unbroken vigilance at every moment and toward everyone, comparing it to the mythical two-necked Bharunda bird that can never relax its watch.
536.tie_back: The Kural praises unfailing watchfulness toward everyone and at all times as the highest good; this verse asks for exactly that constant, all-round alertness.
536.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
536._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). Near one-to-one on vigilance toward all and at all times.

537.quote_or_event: “By conquering his will, (a monk) reaches liberation, as a well-broken horse which is clad in harness (goes to battle). Be watchful in your young years; for thereby a monk quickly obtains liberation.”
537.explanation: Watchfulness and self-control are the means by which even the hardest goal, liberation, is quickly reached.
537.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is too hard for one who works with an unforgetting mind as his tool; Mahavira says watchfulness wins even liberation, the hardest goal of all.
537.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
537._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse concerns liberation rather than worldly tasks, and the mind is not explicitly called a tool.

538.quote_or_event: “He who in this life has done no good actions and has not practised the Law, repents of it in the next world when he has become a prey to Death.”
538.explanation: The monk Kitra warns King Brahmadatta that failing to do what the Law commends brings regret beyond this life.
538.tie_back: Valluvar says those who neglect the deeds the wise have praised find no good in any of their births; Kitra likewise warns that neglecting the Law brings suffering in the next existence.
538.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
538._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on consequences across births; the Kural's 'things the wise have praised' are kingly duties, whereas here they are religious duties.

539.quote_or_event: “And Brahmadatta, king of the Pañkâlas, did not act on the counsel of the saint; he enjoyed the highest pleasure, and (afterwards) sank into the deepest hell.”
539.explanation: The Jain canon holds up Brahmadatta, a universal monarch who stayed absorbed in pleasure and ignored all warnings, as an example of ruin through heedlessness.
539.tie_back: The Kural tells a man swollen with delight to remember those who perished through heedlessness; Brahmadatta is just such a cautionary figure in Jain tradition.
539.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
539._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). Close fit: a powerful king ruined by heedless indulgence.

540.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
540.explanation: Mahavira urges Gautama not to slacken near the goal but to keep his mind steadily on reaching the far shore.
540.tie_back: The Kural says the goal is easily reached if one keeps thinking of it steadily; Mahavira likewise tells Gautama that sustained, unslackening attention completes the crossing.
540.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
540._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com ('&c.' abbreviates the refrain in the original). It is an exhortation to persevere rather than a statement that steady thought makes success easy.
